query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy thin coating, refining the as‐deposited grain structure (e.g., via an enhanced cooling rate during deposition) increases the resistance to high-temperature sliding wear by elevating microhardness, providing more effective grain-boundary pinning of dislocation motion, and promoting the formation of a stable, protective oxide surface layer. This improvement acts through the combined effect of a refined microstructure and stabilized oxide formation under high-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating deposited under conventional cooling conditions resulting in a relatively coarse or moderate grain size and without engineered oxide pre‐formation.
generation.intervention: Increase the cooling rate during deposition (or apply a post-deposition rapid thermal treatment) to refine the grain structure, thereby producing a finer-grained microstructure relative to the baseline condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding contact within the intended operational regime under a constant normal load, where oxidation and thermally activated dislocation motion are significant.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain size with a higher density of grain boundaries and the formation of a more homogeneous, protective oxide layer during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced cooling rate refines the grain structure, which increases microhardness and raises the density of grain boundaries that effectively impede dislocation movement. Under high-temperature sliding conditions, the refined microstructure also promotes the formation of a uniform, adherent oxide layer that protects against adhesive and abrasive wear, thereby limiting microscopic plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The refined-coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient, reduced wear rate, and diminished microscopic plastic deformation compared to the baseline coating under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The conventional FeNiCrCoCu coating produced under standard cooling conditions that presents a coarser microstructure and exhibits higher wear and more prominent plastic deformation during sliding.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected as long as the refined microstructure remains stable during high-temperature exposure. If grain coarsening or oxide layer spallation occurs during prolonged high-temperature sliding, the beneficial effects may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of wear reduction and the durability of the refined microstructure/oxide layer under real operating conditions remain uncertain and may depend on specific thermal gradients, sliding speeds, and oxidation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on identical metal substrates: one using a conventional cooling rate (baseline) and one using an enhanced cooling rate to achieve a finer grain size. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (600–800 °C) under controlled load and sliding speed. Characterize the microstructure (e.g., via SEM/TEM and XRD) before and after testing and measure friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Grain size distribution via electron microscopy
Integrity and adherence of any oxide surface layer (via surface analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced cooling rate (refined) coating does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in microhardness, lower friction coefficient, and reduced wear rate compared to the baseline—with accompanying evidence of a refined microstructure and stable oxide layer—then the hypothesis that grain refinement governs high-temperature wear resistance and deformation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the mechanical properties of FeNiCrCoCu HEA with different atomic ratios are predicted using ML and the optimal principal-element ratio is determined. Then, the tension-compression asymmetry of HEA at different temperatures and components was studied using the MD method. The tension-compression asymmetry of HEAs was revealed through microstructural evolution. To reveal the strengthening effect of HEA on nickel, the influence of HEA coating on the mechanical property of Ni matrix and its microscopic mechanism were further explored.

The following conclusions are drawn based on the analysis of its macroscopic morphology, microscopic morphology, structure, and properties:(1)The FeCoCrNiAlWx HEA cladding coatings mainly consist of FCC solid solution and µ phase. When x = 0.8, the hardness reaches 756.83 HV0.2. The wear resistance of the cladding coating also improves accordingly, with the friction coefficient gradually decreasing. When x = 0.6 and x = 0.8, the friction coefficients are relatively close, with the average friction coefficient reaching a minimum of 0.527.
